hunts.title: Command and Control Periodic Beaconing Detection
hunts.hypothesis: An implant or agent from an adversary C2 framework (e.g. Cobalt Strike, Sliver, Mythic) executes periodic HTTP/HTTPS or TCP beacon check-ins to an external listener, exhibiting low inter-arrival jitter.
hunts.logic_summary: Applies KQL window serialization (serialize and prev) grouped per device, initiating process, and remote destination to calculate the inter-arrival time deltas between outbound connections, computing the coefficient of variation (jitter ratio) to flag regular, low-jitter periodic beaconing.

parameters.name: minConnections
parameters.description: Minimum number of connections required for statistical validity

parameters.name: maxJitterRatio
parameters.description: Experimental threshold for coefficient of variation (stdev / avg); calibrated against synthetic baseline noise

false_positives: Legitimate telemetry heartbeats from commercial software (e.g. cloud storage sync, antivirus update checks)
Network time protocol (NTP) or DNS forwarder lookups running on fixed timers
tuning: Exclude verified enterprise proxy egress points and CDNs (e.g. Microsoft 365, AWS CloudFront, Cloudflare)
Lower maxJitterRatio threshold if noisy benign monitoring agents are triggering alerts (treat thresholds as experimental heuristics)
triage_steps: Inspect RemoteIP and RemoteUrl reputation using threat intelligence lookups (VirusTotal, AlienVault OTX)
Check the InitiatingProcessFileName and full command line of the process responsible for network traffic
Determine if the initiating process is unsigned, running from a temporary directory (e.g. AppData\Local\Temp), or injected
Correlate with process execution and file creation events on the device immediately preceding the start of the beacon
hunts.response: Isolate the endpoint from the network via Defender XDR portal, terminate the beaconing process tree, dump process memory for C2 configuration extraction, and block the remote IP across corporate perimeter firewalls.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1071 Application Layer Protocol
Hunting for C2 Beacons using KQL

hunts.query:
// Hunt: HB-C2-001 - Command and Control Periodic Beaconing Detection
// MITRE ATT&CK: T1071 (Application Layer Protocol)
// Platform: Microsoft Defender XDR (DeviceNetworkEvents)
//
// Description: Detects regular interval network callbacks (beacons) from endpoint processes
// to external remote IPs by calculating inter-connection time deltas and the coefficient of
// variation (jitter ratio) using KQL window serialization (serialize and prev) grouped per process.

let lookback = 24h;
let minConnections = 15;
let maxJitterRatio = 0.35;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where not(ipv4_is_private(RemoteIP))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| sort by DeviceName asc, InitiatingProcessFileName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| serialize
| extend PrevDevice = prev(DeviceName),
         PrevProc = prev(InitiatingProcessFileName),
         PrevIP = prev(RemoteIP),
         PrevPort = prev(RemotePort),
         PrevTime = prev(Timestamp)
| extend TimeDelta = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, PrevTime)
| where DeviceName == PrevDevice 
    and InitiatingProcessFileName == PrevProc 
    and RemoteIP == PrevIP 
    and RemotePort == PrevPort 
    and TimeDelta > 0
| summarize 
    FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
    LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
    TotalConnections = count(),
    AvgDelta = avg(TimeDelta),
    StdDevDelta = stdev(TimeDelta),
    MinDelta = min(TimeDelta),
    MaxDelta = max(TimeDelta),
    RemoteUrls = make_set(RemoteUrl, 3)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where TotalConnections >= minConnections
| extend JitterRatio = iff(AvgDelta > 0, round(StdDevDelta / AvgDelta, 3), 1.0)
| where JitterRatio <= maxJitterRatio
| project FirstSeen, LastSeen, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrls,
          TotalConnections, AvgDelta, StdDevDelta, JitterRatio
| order by JitterRatio asc, TotalConnections desc

hunts.title: Anomalous burst of cloud file downloads from SharePoint or OneDrive
hunts.hypothesis: An adversary with compromised credentials or a malicious insider rapidly downloads a significant volume of documents, spreadsheets, or source code from SharePoint or OneDrive prior to extortion or data theft.
hunts.logic_summary: Aggregates FileDownloaded actions across SharePoint and OneDrive in 1-hour tumbling windows per user account, flagging any account exceeding the threshold of 50 downloads within a single window.

parameters.name: window
parameters.description: Tumbling time bucket window for grouping download spikes

parameters.name: minDownloads
parameters.description: Minimum number of file downloads required to trigger a lead

false_positives: Users syncing a large newly shared SharePoint folder or migrating local files using the OneDrive sync client
Automated enterprise data backup or DLP scanning service accounts
tuning: Exclude verified enterprise service accounts and migration tooling service principals
Raise the minDownloads threshold for departments that legitimately perform high-volume batch processing
triage_steps: Inspect the SampleFiles list to see what sensitive keywords or document types (e.g. financials, contracts, patents) were downloaded
Check whether the downloads originated from a managed corporate device or an unmanaged personal device / anonymous proxy
Review HR status to determine if the user has recently submitted a resignation or has pending disciplinary action
hunts.response: Temporarily restrict the user's SharePoint access via Conditional Access or session controls, engage the user's manager and legal/insider risk team, and preserve DLP audit trails.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1530 Data from Cloud Storage
Microsoft Defender Advanced Hunting CloudAppEvents

hunts.query:
// HB-CL-001 | T1530 | Anomalous burst of cloud file downloads
// Hypothesis: An attacker or departing insider rapidly downloads a large volume of files from cloud storage (SharePoint / OneDrive) for exfiltration.
let lookback = 1d;
let window = 1h;
let minDownloads = 50;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where Application in~ ("Microsoft SharePoint Online", "Microsoft OneDrive for Business")
| where ActionType =~ "FileDownloaded"
| summarize
    DownloadCount = count(),
    FirstDownload = min(Timestamp),
    LastDownload = max(Timestamp),
    SampleFiles = make_set(tostring(ActivityObjects), 10)
    by AccountDisplayName, AccountId, IPAddress, CountryCode, bin(Timestamp, window)
| where DownloadCount >= minDownloads
| project
    Timestamp,
    AccountDisplayName,
    AccountId,
    DownloadCount,
    IPAddress,
    CountryCode,
    FirstDownload,
    LastDownload,
    SampleFiles
| order by DownloadCount desc

hunts.title: OAuth application consent or service principal granted sensitive scopes
hunts.hypothesis: An adversary executes an Illicit Consent Grant (T1528) tricking users into authorizing permissions, or abuses compromised administrative privileges to register rogue service principals and delegated grants (T1098) with high-privilege Microsoft Graph API scopes (e.g. Mail.ReadWrite, Files.ReadWrite.All) for persistent exfiltration.
hunts.logic_summary: Monitors Entra ID AuditLogs for successful application management events, categorizing direct consent grants (T1528) versus service principal creations and delegated grants (T1098), filtering for sensitive data access permissions.
false_positives: Legitimate enterprise integrations configured by IT administrators (e.g. DocuSign, Slack, Salesforce)
Approved developer sandbox applications created in internal Azure subscriptions
tuning: Restrict user consent policies in Entra ID so standard users cannot consent to unverified multi-tenant apps
Whitelist pre-approved corporate enterprise applications by verified Microsoft Publisher ID
triage_steps: Check the AppDisplayName and verified publisher domain in the Microsoft Entra admin center
Identify who consented to the application and what specific permissions were granted
Search SigninLogs and CloudAppEvents for API activities executed by the application Service Principal
hunts.response: Revoke the application's consent immediately via Entra ID (Enterprise Applications -> Permissions -> Revoke), delete the service principal, and investigate user mailbox audit logs for exfiltration.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1528 Steal Application Access Token
Detect and Remediate Illicit Consent Grants in Microsoft 365

hunts.query:
// HB-CL-002 | T1528 / T1098 | OAuth application consent & permission grant with sensitive scopes
// Hypothesis: An attacker conducts an Illicit Consent Grant (T1528) or creates a rogue Service Principal / Permission Grant (T1098)
// to gain persistent API access to emails, user directories, and cloud files without requiring interactive user credentials.
let lookback = 7d;
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Category =~ "ApplicationManagement"
| where OperationName in~ (
    "Consent to application",
    "Add delegated permission grant",
    "Add service principal"
)
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend TargetJson = tostring(TargetResources)
| where TargetJson has_any (
    "Mail.Read", "Mail.ReadWrite", "MailboxSettings.ReadWrite",
    "Files.ReadWrite.All", "offline_access", "User.ReadWrite.All"
)
| extend ActionCategory = case(
    OperationName has "Consent", "User / Admin Consent Grant (T1528)",
    OperationName has "service principal", "Service Principal Registration (T1098)",
    OperationName has "delegated permission", "Delegated Permission Grant (T1098)",
    "Application Management"
)
| extend AppDisplayName = coalesce(tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName), tostring(TargetResources[0].modifiedProperties[0].newValue))
| extend AppId = tostring(TargetResources[0].id)
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| project
    TimeGenerated,
    ActionCategory,
    OperationName,
    AppDisplayName,
    AppId,
    Actor,
    TargetJson,
    ResultDescription
| order by TimeGenerated desc

hunts.title: Sign-in from Known Anonymizer or Tor Exit Node
hunts.hypothesis: An adversary routes authentication attempts through Tor exit nodes or commercial anonymizers (T1090) to conceal their true geographic origin and bypass geo-blocking Conditional Access policies while attempting to authenticate with compromised Valid Accounts (T1078). In isolation, VPN traffic can be benign; it becomes actionable when paired with unusual sign-in hours, failure clusters, or sensitive app access.
hunts.logic_summary: Filters Entra ID SigninLogs for events where RiskDetail indicates an anonymous IP or Tor exit node, or where NetworkLocationDetails matches anonymizer tags, summarizing success versus failure counts per identity.
false_positives: Corporate employees using approved commercial privacy VPNs or cellular carrier networks with shared proxy egress
Authorized security teams conducting external penetration tests or simulated red team engagements
tuning: Filter out verified enterprise corporate VPN egress CIDRs and authorized secure web gateway egress IPs
Require Conditional Access location enforcement that strictly blocks non-compliant network locations
triage_steps: Verify if the sign-in was successful (ResultType == 0) or failed (ResultType != 0)
Examine the user's typical login locations and devices using Entra ID sign-in history
Review whether multi-factor authentication was satisfied during the session
Check for anomalous cloud resource access or inbox rule modifications directly following this session
hunts.response: If unauthorized success is confirmed, revoke all active user refresh tokens via Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken, force a password reset, and enable strict Conditional Access policies blocking untrusted anonymous IPs.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1090 Proxy
Microsoft Entra ID Protection Risk Detections

hunts.title: Azure Resource Deletion Burst
hunts.hypothesis: An adversary with compromised Azure administrative credentials or a rogue employee initiates a mass deletion of critical cloud infrastructure (VMs, storage accounts, databases, or key vaults) to paralyze business operations.
hunts.logic_summary: Aggregates AzureActivity control plane events with OperationNameValue ending in '/delete' and status 'Success', grouping by Caller identity and 30-minute time buckets to flag accounts deleting 3 or more resources in rapid succession.

parameters.name: burstWindow
parameters.description: Grouping window for identifying rapid deletion bursts

parameters.name: deletionThreshold
parameters.description: Minimum number of deletions within the window to trigger an alert

false_positives: Automated CI/CD teardown pipelines cleaning up ephemeral test environments
Terraform or ARM template deployments destroying and recreating infrastructure
tuning: Whitelist dedicated automation service principals used by authorized deployment pipelines
Scope alerts specifically to production subscriptions where mass deletions are never normal
triage_steps: Identify the Caller identity (UPN or AppId) and verify if the action was part of an approved change ticket
Inspect CallerIpAddress against known corporate locations or VPN gateways
Review the specific resources deleted and check if Azure Soft Delete or backup snapshots can restore them
Check AzureActivity for prior privilege escalation or role assignment events involving this identity
hunts.response: If unauthorized, immediately disable the user account or revoke the service principal credentials in Entra ID, lock down Azure subscription management permissions, and initiate cloud disaster recovery procedures.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1485 Data Destruction
Azure Activity Log Operations Reference

hunts.title: Inbound email delivered with high-risk executable or script attachment
hunts.hypothesis: An adversary sends spearphishing emails carrying container files (ISO, VHD) or standalone scripts (HTA, LNK, VBS) to evade Mark-of-the-Web (MOTW) protections and execute malicious downloaders.
hunts.logic_summary: Searches EmailAttachmentInfo in Defender for Office 365 for inbound delivered emails with high-risk attachment file types typically abused in initial access campaigns.
false_positives: Rare legitimate developer communications sharing script snippets or IT administration tools
Software vendor distribution of installation disk images (ISOs) to technical staff
tuning: Block high-risk file types outright at the Defender for Office 365 tenant transport rule level
Allow-list trusted business partner sender domains verified via SPF, DKIM, and DMARC
triage_steps: Check whether the recipient user opened or saved the attachment to disk using DeviceFileEvents
Inspect the SHA256 file hash in Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence and VirusTotal
Search EmailEvents for other employees in the organization who received the same NetworkMessageId
hunts.response: Purge the email message across all inboxes using Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Explorer / ZAP, block the sender domain, and isolate the endpoint if execution occurred.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1566.001 Phishing - Spearphishing Attachment
Microsoft Defender Advanced Hunting EmailAttachmentInfo

hunts.query:
// HB-EM-001 | T1566.001 | Inbound email delivered with high-risk executable or script attachment
// Hypothesis: An attacker delivers phishing emails containing weaponized container files (ISO, VHD) or scripts (HTA, LNK, JS) to bypass gateway defenses.
let lookback = 7d;
EmailAttachmentInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where FileType in~ (
    "iso", "vhd", "hta", "lnk", "js", "vbs", "ps1", "wsf", "scr", "jar", "bat", "cmd"
)
| project
    Timestamp,
    NetworkMessageId,
    SenderFromAddress,
    RecipientEmailAddress,
    FileName,
    FileType,
    SHA256,
    ThreatTypes,
    DetectionMethods
| order by Timestamp desc

hunts.title: Safe Links click on potential phishing URL or warning dismissed
hunts.hypothesis: An employee clicks an inbound email phishing link where Microsoft Defender Safe Links either permitted navigation or the user explicitly bypassed a red security warning screen to reach the destination.
hunts.logic_summary: Monitors UrlClickEvents in Defender for Office 365 for ClickAllowed on URLs determined to be Phish/Malware or user clicks where WarningDismissed indicates deliberate override of security controls.
false_positives: Legitimate corporate marketing or HR survey URLs incorrectly classified by automated reputation feeds
Authorized internal phishing awareness simulation campaigns (e.g. KnowBe4, Defender Attack Simulation)
tuning: Exclude verified internal authorized phishing simulation header IDs or sender IPs
Whitelist internal domain single sign-on URLs and verified SaaS portals
triage_steps: Review the destination URL to determine if it mimics a Microsoft 365 login page or contains a file download
Check SigninLogs for subsequent sign-ins from the user's IP or foreign IPs within the next 4 hours
Interview the user to determine if they submitted credentials or downloaded any files
hunts.response: Block the URL tenant-wide using the Tenant Allow/Block List (TABL), reset the user's password, revoke active sessions, and verify MFA device registrations.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1566.002 Phishing - Spearphishing Link
Microsoft Defender Advanced Hunting UrlClickEvents

hunts.query:
// HB-EM-002 | T1566.002 | Safe Links click on potential phishing URL or warning dismissed
// Hypothesis: A user clicks an inbound email link to an external phishing or credential-harvesting site, potentially entering credentials or downloading malware.
let lookback = 7d;
UrlClickEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where ActionType in~ ("ClickAllowed", "WarningDismissed")
| where ThreatTypes in~ ("Phish", "Malware")
     or (ClickType =~ "WarningDismissed")
| project
    Timestamp,
    AccountUpn,
    IPAddress,
    Url,
    ClickType,
    ActionType,
    ThreatTypes,
    NetworkMessageId
| order by Timestamp desc

hunts.title: Suspicious email inbox rule created to forward or delete messages
hunts.hypothesis: An attacker who gains unauthorized access to a victim mailbox configures hidden inbox forwarding or auto-deletion rules to silently exfiltrate sensitive corporate communications or hide password reset and security alerts.
hunts.logic_summary: Queries CloudAppEvents for Microsoft Exchange Online inbox rule creation or modification events where the parameters specify external forwarding, redirecting, or automatic deletion/marking as read.
false_positives: Legitimate employees configuring vacation out-of-office forwards to internal teammates or corporate shared mailboxes
Users organizing high-volume notification emails into designated subfolders
tuning: Whitelist internal corporate domain recipient addresses (e.g. *@contoso.com) to alert only on external forwarding rules
Correlate with SigninLogs to suppress if created from a known Intune compliant device in the user's typical home location
triage_steps: Extract the destination email address from the Parameters string to see where emails are being forwarded
Check whether the IPAddress that created the rule matches the user's usual work location or an anomalous country/VPN
Search SigninLogs for recent failed or anomalous logins for the same AccountId
hunts.response: Remove the malicious inbox rule via Exchange Online PowerShell (Remove-InboxRule), revoke all active sessions for the user, reset account credentials, and inspect sent items for fraudulent financial requests.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1114.003 Email Collection - Email Forwarding Rule
Detect and Remediate Illicit Consent and Rule Grants

hunts.query:
// HB-EM-003 | T1114.003 | Suspicious email inbox rule created to forward or delete messages
// Hypothesis: An attacker with compromised mailbox access creates inbox rules to exfiltrate emails or hide detection notices by forwarding or deleting incoming messages.
let lookback = 7d;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where Application =~ "Microsoft Exchange Online"
| where ActionType in~ ("New-InboxRule", "Set-InboxRule", "UpdateInboxRules")
| extend RuleParameters = coalesce(
    tostring(RawEventData.Parameters),
    tostring(RawEventData.ModifiedProperties),
    tostring(RawEventData)
)
| where RuleParameters has_any (
    "ForwardTo", "ForwardAsAttachmentTo", "RedirectTo",
    "DeleteMessage", "MoveToFolder", "MarkAsRead"
)
| project
    Timestamp,
    AccountDisplayName,
    AccountId,
    ActionType,
    IPAddress,
    CountryCode,
    City,
    RuleParameters,
    UserAgent
| order by Timestamp desc

hunts.title: Office application spawning script interpreter or shell
hunts.hypothesis: An adversary delivers a weaponized Office attachment (docm, xlsm) via spearphishing. While T1204.002 describes the initial user execution of the document, this detection identifies the subsequent Command and Scripting Interpreter execution (T1059.001) where embedded VBA macro code or an exploit spawns cmd.exe, powershell.exe, or mshta.exe.
hunts.logic_summary: Inspects DeviceProcessEvents in Defender for Endpoint where the parent process (InitiatingProcessFileName) is a Microsoft Office application and the newly spawned child process is an interactive shell or script engine.
false_positives: Legitimate enterprise accounting or financial spreadsheets utilizing complex approved VBA macros that call cmd.exe for internal scripts
Add-ins from security software, Adobe Acrobat, or document management systems
tuning: Allow-list verified corporate Excel macro add-ins by filtering on specific InitiatingProcessCommandLine patterns or digital signature status
Restrict child interpreters to specific untrusted directories or unusual command-line flags
triage_steps: Review the OfficeCommandLine to identify the file name and path of the document that was opened
Inspect the ProcessCommandLine to see what script or remote URL the child interpreter attempted to run
Check DeviceFileEvents and DeviceNetworkEvents for the same DeviceId around the same Timestamp
hunts.response: Isolate the affected endpoint via Defender for Endpoint APIs, collect the suspicious document for malware analysis, and search email gateway logs for other recipients of the same attachment.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1204.002 User Execution - Malicious File
Microsoft Defender Advanced Hunting DeviceProcessEvents

hunts.query:
// HB-EP-001 | T1204.002 | Office application spawning script interpreter or shell
// Hypothesis: An attacker executes code on an endpoint via a malicious macro or document exploit that spawns an interactive shell or script engine.
let lookback = 7d;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winword.exe", "excel.exe", "powerpnt.exe", "outlook.exe", "onenote.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "mshta.exe", "bash.exe")
| project
    Timestamp,
    DeviceName,
    AccountName,
    OfficeApp = InitiatingProcessFileName,
    OfficeCommandLine = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
    SpawnedInterpreter = FileName,
    ProcessCommandLine,
    ProcessIntegrityLevel,
    InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

hunts.title: PowerShell executed with Base64 encoded command arguments
hunts.hypothesis: An adversary executes Base64-encoded PowerShell payloads to bypass signature-based endpoint defenses, obfuscate remote download cradles, or execute in-memory shellcode runners.
hunts.logic_summary: Queries DeviceProcessEvents for powershell.exe or pwsh.exe where the command-line parameters contain encoded argument flags (-e, -enc, -encodedcommand) followed by a Base64 string of at least 30 characters.

parameters.name: minEncodedLength
parameters.description: Minimum length of the Base64 string payload to filter trivial flags

false_positives: Enterprise systems management tools (Microsoft Endpoint Configuration Manager / SCCM, Intune, Tanium)
Software deployment installers and monitoring agents executing pre-packaged health checks
tuning: Filter out approved management parent processes (e.g. CcmExec.exe, taniumclient.exe)
Exclude known benign script command lines signed by internal enterprise certificates
triage_steps: Extract the Base64 encoded payload and decode it (UTF-16LE / Unicode) in a sandbox or CyberChef
Inspect the decoded command for download cradles (e.g. IEX, Net.WebClient, Invoke-RestMethod) or credential access
Identify the parent process and account that initiated the PowerShell command
hunts.response: Terminate the malicious process, isolate the endpoint if remote connections or secondary payloads are detected, and block any remote command and control (C2) domains identified in the decoded payload.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1059.001 Command and Scripting Interpreter - PowerShell
Microsoft Defender Advanced Hunting DeviceProcessEvents

hunts.query:
// HB-EP-002 | T1059.001 | PowerShell executed with Base64 encoded command arguments
// Hypothesis: An attacker uses Base64 encoded PowerShell commands (-enc, -encodedcommand) to obfuscate malicious payloads and evade simple command-line string matching.
let lookback = 7d;
let minEncodedLength = 30;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s-(e|enc|encodedcommand)\s+[A-Za-z0-9+/=]{30,}"
| project
    Timestamp,
    DeviceName,
    AccountName,
    FileName,
    ProcessCommandLine,
    InitiatingProcessFileName,
    InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
    FolderPath,
    SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

hunts.title: Ingress tool transfer via LOLBins (certutil, bitsadmin)
hunts.hypothesis: An adversary leverages built-in, trusted Microsoft utilities (LOLBins) such as certutil.exe or bitsadmin.exe to download malicious binaries or scripts directly from remote staging servers without raising traditional perimeter alarms.
hunts.logic_summary: Filters DeviceProcessEvents for executions of certutil.exe or bitsadmin.exe containing command-line switches indicative of remote URL fetching (-urlcache, -split, /transfer) and extracts the remote destination URL.
false_positives: Legitimate IT admin maintenance scripts downloading CRL (Certificate Revocation Lists) using certutil
Windows update background jobs utilizing BITS for legitimate patch distribution
tuning: Whitelist internal corporate PKI certificate distribution endpoints (e.g. *.corp.contoso.com)
Exclude executions running under the NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM account targeting known Microsoft CRL endpoints
triage_steps: Review the ExtractedUrl to determine the domain reputation, hosting provider, and file extension
Search DeviceFileEvents for files written to disk by the parent or child process around that timestamp
Check whether the downloaded file was subsequently executed in DeviceProcessEvents
hunts.response: Block the remote URL and domain at the proxy/firewall level, quarantine the downloaded artifact on the host, and submit the file hash to Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence for organization-wide sweeping.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer
LOLBAS Project - Certutil

hunts.query:
// HB-EP-003 | T1105 | Ingress tool transfer via LOLBins (certutil, bitsadmin)
// Hypothesis: An attacker uses legitimate native Windows utilities to download external payloads, evading typical egress restrictions.
let lookback = 7d;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where FileName in~ ("certutil.exe", "bitsadmin.exe")
| where (FileName =~ "certutil.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-urlcache", "/urlcache", "-split", "/split"))
     or (FileName =~ "bitsadmin.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/transfer", "/create", "/addfile"))
| extend ExtractedUrl = extract(@"https?://[^\s""']+", 0, ProcessCommandLine)
| project
    Timestamp,
    DeviceName,
    AccountName,
    FileName,
    ProcessCommandLine,
    ExtractedUrl,
    InitiatingProcessFileName,
    InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
    FolderPath,
    SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

hunts.title: Suspicious process access targeting LSASS memory for credential dumping
hunts.hypothesis: An attacker accesses the LSASS process with high-privilege read access via Windows APIs (MiniDumpWriteDump, OpenProcess) to extract NTLM password hashes or Kerberos tickets from memory.
hunts.logic_summary: Filters DeviceEvents for OpenProcessApiCall where the target process is lsass.exe and the initiating parent process is not a standard Windows OS component or security agent.
false_positives: Legitimate third-party endpoint protection, backup software, or performance diagnostics agents
Security vulnerability scanners performing credential audit checks
tuning: Allow-list trusted third-party security agents verified by digital code signing certificates
Exclude known IT administrative diagnostic tools executed from approved system directories
triage_steps: Identify the InitiatingProcessCommandLine and check where the binary is running from
Check DeviceFileEvents for new .dmp or .tmp files created on the host around the same time
Search DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound connections from the same device
hunts.response: Isolate the endpoint immediately via Defender for Endpoint API, terminate the offending process, and rotate passwords and Kerberos tickets (krbtgt) for any users logged into that endpoint.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1003.001 OS Credential Dumping - LSASS Memory
Microsoft Defender Advanced Hunting DeviceEvents

hunts.query:
// HB-EP-004 | T1003.001 | Suspicious process access targeting LSASS memory for credential dumping
// Hypothesis: An attacker opens a handle to the lsass.exe process from an unusual utility or script to dump memory and harvest plaintext passwords or Kerberos tickets.
let lookback = 7d;
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where ActionType in~ ("OpenProcessApiCall", "ProcessAccess")
| extend TargetProc = coalesce(FileName, tostring(AdditionalFields.TargetProcessFileName))
| where TargetProc =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ (
    "csrss.exe", "svchost.exe", "MsMpEng.exe", "Sense.exe",
    "winlogon.exe", "lsass.exe", "services.exe"
)
| extend DesiredAccess = tostring(AdditionalFields.DesiredAccess)
| project
    Timestamp,
    DeviceName,
    AccountName,
    TargetProcess = TargetProc,
    DesiredAccess,
    InitiatingProcessFileName,
    InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
    AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc

hunts.title: Microsoft Defender Antivirus exclusion added
hunts.hypothesis: An adversary with local admin privileges tampers with Windows Defender Antivirus exclusions to carve out directories (e.g. C:\Temp, C:\Users\Public) where secondary malware tools can run unhindered.
hunts.logic_summary: Detects modifications and key creations in DeviceRegistryEvents under the Microsoft\Windows Defender\Exclusions registry branch.
false_positives: Legitimate enterprise IT deployment scripts configuring performance exclusions for databases or developer tooling
Antivirus configuration deployed via Microsoft Intune or Group Policy Objects (GPO)
tuning: Exclude changes initiated by svchost.exe running under the NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM account from verified Intune policies
Alert immediately if the excluded path is a user-writable directory (e.g. \AppData\, \Users\Public\, \Temp\)
triage_steps: Inspect RegistryValueName and RegistryValueData to see which specific path or file extension was excluded
Review the InitiatingProcessCommandLine to see if PowerShell (Add-MpPreference) or reg.exe was used
Search DeviceFileEvents for files created inside the newly excluded path
hunts.response: Remove the unauthorized exclusion via PowerShell (Remove-MpPreference), initiate a full Microsoft Defender antivirus scan, and investigate the host for dropped payloads.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1562.001 Impair Defenses - Disable or Modify Tools
Configure Exclusions in Microsoft Defender Antivirus

hunts.query:
// HB-EP-005 | T1562.001 | Microsoft Defender Antivirus exclusion added
// Hypothesis: An attacker adds folder or file exclusions to Windows Defender to prevent detection of malware payloads dropped onto the endpoint.
let lookback = 7d;
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where ActionType in~ ("RegistryValueSet", "RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"Microsoft\Windows Defender\Exclusions"
| project
    Timestamp,
    DeviceName,
    RegistryKey,
    RegistryValueName,
    RegistryValueData,
    InitiatingProcessFileName,
    InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
    InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

hunts.title: Windows security or system event log cleared
hunts.hypothesis: An adversary executes anti-forensic commands via wevtutil or PowerShell to wipe Security, System, or PowerShell event logs, covering their tracks following lateral movement or credential theft.
hunts.logic_summary: Monitors DeviceEvents for the EventLogCleared action type or process executions of wevtutil.exe invoking clear-log (cl) commands.
false_positives: Routine system maintenance scripts in dedicated test labs or automated virtual machine image build pipelines
Highly uncommon automated IT log rotation scripts
tuning: Whitelist dedicated automated Golden Image build environments (e.g. Packer / Azure Image Builder)
Alert immediately on any production server or domain controller clearing the Security log
triage_steps: Identify which specific log was cleared (Security, System, PowerShellCore, etc.)
Review the user account and initiating command line that executed the clear command
Examine previous activities performed on that host prior to the log deletion
hunts.response: Isolate the endpoint immediately, preserve forensic RAM and disk artifacts, and treat the event as active compromise.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1070.001 Indicator Removal on Host - Clear Windows Event Logs
Microsoft Defender Advanced Hunting DeviceEvents

hunts.query:
// HB-EP-006 | T1070.001 | Windows security or system event log cleared
// Hypothesis: An attacker uses wevtutil or PowerShell to clear Windows event logs to destroy forensic evidence of malicious activity.
let lookback = 7d;
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where ActionType =~ "EventLogCleared"
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "wevtutil.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("cl", "clear-log"))
| project
    Timestamp,
    DeviceName,
    AccountName,
    ActionType,
    InitiatingProcessFileName,
    InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
    AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc

hunts.title: Password spray against multiple accounts from a single IP
hunts.hypothesis: An adversary attempts a small list of commonly used passwords (e.g. SeasonYear!, Welcome123) against dozens or hundreds of different user accounts from a single source IP to remain under the smart lockout threshold of individual accounts.
hunts.logic_summary: Filters SigninLogs for failed authentications caused by invalid credentials (ResultType 50126), groups them by source IP address into tumbling time windows (bin), and flags any single IP that hits a threshold of distinct user accounts (dcount).

parameters.name: window
parameters.description: Tumbling time bucket window for grouping spray attempts

parameters.name: minUsers
parameters.description: Minimum number of unique accounts targeted to trigger a hunting lead

parameters.name: followUpWindow
parameters.description: Window following spray failures to correlate successful sign-ins

false_positives: Corporate egress proxies or shared NAT gateways where multiple employees misconfigure credentials simultaneously
Enterprise single sign-on (SSO) cutover, active directory sync jobs, or mass password reset days
tuning: Exclude verified corporate external NAT egress IP ranges or VPN gateways using a Sentinel watchlist
Increase the minUsers threshold in large enterprise environments (>5,000 active users) to 25 or 50
triage_steps: Check whether any account targeted by this IP had a subsequent successful login (ResultType 0)
Examine the source IP threat reputation, ISP, ASN, and user agent string for automation fingerprints
Determine if the targeted accounts belong to privileged roles (e.g. Global Admins, Conditional Access Admins)
hunts.response: Block the attacking IP address on perimeter firewalls / Conditional Access named locations, and trigger an immediate password reset and session revocation for any user that logged in successfully.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1110.003 Password Spraying
Microsoft Entra Sign-in Error Codes (50126)

hunts.title: Targeted brute force against a single account followed by success
hunts.hypothesis: An attacker focuses an aggressive password brute-force attack against a specific executive or admin account from a single source IP, successfully guessing the password within an hour.
hunts.logic_summary: Groups SigninLogs by user and source IP in 1-hour tumbling windows, counting failed logins (50126) and successful logins (0), alerting when failures exceed threshold and are immediately followed by a successful login.

parameters.name: minFailures
parameters.description: Minimum number of failed attempts prior to success

parameters.name: followUpWindow
parameters.description: Window following brute-force failures to correlate subsequent successful sign-in

false_positives: A user who recently changed their password on their phone/laptop and forgot to update cached credentials on other apps
Automated enterprise sync service accounts experiencing temporary authentication desync
tuning: Correlate with AppDisplayName to exclude automated mobile device sync (e.g. Apple Internet Accounts)
Allow-list internal trusted office network IP ranges
triage_steps: Verify whether the user was legitimately attempting to log in during that hour
Review the IP geolocation and threat reputation to determine if the source IP is external or a commercial proxy
Check whether subsequent actions were performed in Azure AD / Microsoft 365 by the newly logged-in session
hunts.response: Revoke the session immediately via Entra ID, enforce a mandatory password reset, and investigate endpoint telemetry for evidence of subsequent lateral movement.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1110 Brute Force
Microsoft Entra Password Protection & Smart Lockout

hunts.title: Impossible travel sign-ins from distant locations in unrealistic time
hunts.hypothesis: An adversary is authenticating using compromised valid credentials from a different country or cloud provider hosting site while the authentic employee is concurrently active from their home region.
hunts.logic_summary: Tracks consecutive successful sign-ins per user, orders chronologically, calculates the time delta between different geographic locations using serialize and prev(), and flags logins where the speed required to travel between the locations exceeds physical limits (e.g. < 60 minutes between countries).

parameters.name: maxTravelHours
parameters.description: Maximum allowable time difference between consecutive logins

parameters.name: maxAirplaneSpeedKph
parameters.description: Maximum plausible commercial airliner speed threshold in km/h

false_positives: Users connecting to or disconnecting from enterprise VPN gateways or zero-trust reverse proxies
Cloud service principal / app proxy logins executing on behalf of users in international Azure datacenters
tuning: Exclude corporate VPN egress gateways and known SaaS proxy networks using a Sentinel watchlist
Correlate with DeviceDetail to suppress if both sign-ins originate from the same Intune-managed device ID
triage_steps: Review the UserAgent and DeviceDetail for both sign-ins to see if one is a recognized work device and the other is unknown
Check whether MFA was completed for the suspicious sign-in or if conditional access was bypassed
Contact the affected user directly via out-of-band communication (phone/Slack) to verify their current physical location
hunts.response: Immediately revoke all active refresh tokens for the user in Entra ID, trigger an interactive MFA prompt, and temporarily disable the account if unauthorized access is confirmed.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1078 Valid Accounts
Microsoft Entra Identity Protection Anomalous Travel

hunts.query:
// Hunt: HB-ID-003 - Impossible Travel Between Distant Regions
// MITRE ATT&CK: T1078 (Valid Accounts)
// Platform: Microsoft Sentinel (SigninLogs)
//
// Description: Detects consecutive successful sign-ins for the same identity from distant
// geographic locations within an unrealistic timeframe, calculating geodesic distance and
// implied travel speed (> 800 km/h), with country-delta fallback for missing coordinates.

let lookback = 1d;
let maxTravelHours = 24.0;
let maxAirplaneSpeedKph = 800.0;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where ResultType == "0" // Only successful sign-ins represent actual session establishment
| where isnotempty(UserPrincipalName)
| extend IdentityKey = coalesce(UserId, UserPrincipalName)
| extend Lat = todouble(LocationDetails.geoCoordinates.latitude),
         Lon = todouble(LocationDetails.geoCoordinates.longitude)
| project TimeGenerated, IdentityKey, UserId, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, Location, Lat, Lon, AppDisplayName, UserAgent
| order by IdentityKey asc, TimeGenerated asc
| serialize
| extend PrevIdentity = prev(IdentityKey),
         PrevLocation = prev(Location),
         PrevIP = prev(IPAddress),
         PrevTime = prev(TimeGenerated),
         PrevApp = prev(AppDisplayName),
         PrevLat = prev(Lat),
         PrevLon = prev(Lon)
| where IdentityKey == PrevIdentity and IPAddress != PrevIP
| extend TimeDeltaHours = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, PrevTime) / 3600.0
| where TimeDeltaHours > 0 and TimeDeltaHours <= maxTravelHours
| extend CalculatedDistanceKm = iff(
    isnotnull(Lat) and isnotnull(PrevLat) and (Lat != PrevLat or Lon != PrevLon),
    geo_distance_2points(Lat, Lon, PrevLat, PrevLon) / 1000.0,
    real(null)
)
| extend TravelSpeedKph = iff(TimeDeltaHours > 0 and isnotnull(CalculatedDistanceKm), round(CalculatedDistanceKm / TimeDeltaHours, 1), real(null))
| where TravelSpeedKph > maxAirplaneSpeedKph 
    or (isnull(TravelSpeedKph) and Location != PrevLocation and TimeDeltaHours <= 1.0)
| project TimeGenerated, PrevTime, UserPrincipalName, UserId,
          CurrentLocation = Location, PrevLocation,
          CurrentIP = IPAddress, PrevIP,
          CalculatedDistanceKm, TimeDeltaHours, TravelSpeedKph,
          CurrentApp = AppDisplayName, PrevApp, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

hunts.title: Multi-factor authentication fatigue attack followed by success
hunts.hypothesis: An adversary with valid credentials spams MFA push prompts to the victim's mobile device until the fatigued user clicks approve or enters a verification code.
hunts.logic_summary: Aggregates SigninLogs for Entra ID MFA failures (code 500121) grouped by user in 20-minute windows, alerting when 3 or more denials occur immediately before a successful login.

parameters.name: window
parameters.description: Tumbling time bucket window for grouping fatigue prompts

parameters.name: minDenials
parameters.description: Minimum number of MFA prompt denials required

parameters.name: followUpWindow
parameters.description: Sliding window following fatigue prompts to correlate subsequent successful login

false_positives: Flaky mobile cellular connectivity causing multiple failed authentication attempts
A user repeatedly denying an MFA prompt because they did not recognize the prompt, then realizing it was legitimate
tuning: Enforce Entra ID number matching to eliminate blind push approvals
Correlate source IP: alert primarily if the successful login originates from an IP different from the user's regular device
triage_steps: Contact the employee to ask if they approved an unexpected MFA prompt
Check the source IP and geolocation of the successful login
Review AuditLogs for privileged changes made during the newly authenticated session
hunts.response: Revoke all active refresh tokens for the user in Entra ID, reset credentials, and enable strict FIDO2/Passkey MFA.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1621 Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
Defending Against MFA Fatigue Attacks

hunts.title: Successful sign-in using legacy authentication protocols bypassing MFA
hunts.hypothesis: An attacker deliberately authenticates via legacy mail protocols (IMAP, POP3, SMTP) that do not enforce modern multi-factor authentication (MFA) prompts to access email mailboxes with compromised user passwords.
hunts.logic_summary: Scans SigninLogs for successful authentications (ResultType 0) where the client application or user-agent indicates legacy authentication protocols.
false_positives: Legacy multi-function printers, scanners, or on-premises ticketing systems authenticating via SMTP
Rare unmanaged mobile email clients configured by legacy employees
tuning: Block legacy authentication completely in Entra ID Conditional Access policies
Whitelist dedicated corporate scan-to-email static IP addresses
triage_steps: Check whether the account is an interactive human user or an automated service account
Review the source IP address for external hosting providers or overseas geolocations
Search for mailbox export or bulk message download activity following the legacy login
hunts.response: Disable legacy authentication on the user account, enforce modern auth, and revoke active tokens.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1078 Valid Accounts
Blocking Legacy Authentication in Microsoft Entra ID

hunts.query:
// HB-ID-005 | T1078 | Successful sign-in using legacy authentication protocols bypassing MFA
// Hypothesis: An attacker uses legacy authentication protocols (e.g. IMAP, POP3, SMTP) that do not support modern MFA to authenticate using stolen credentials.
let lookback = 7d;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where ResultType == "0"
| where UserAgent has_any ("IMAP", "POP3", "SMTP", "MAPI", "BAV2ROPC", "Exchange ActiveSync")
     or AppDisplayName has_any ("IMAP", "POP", "SMTP")
| project
    TimeGenerated,
    UserPrincipalName,
    IPAddress,
    Location,
    AppDisplayName,
    UserAgent,
    ConditionalAccessStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

hunts.title: Highly privileged directory role assigned in Entra ID
hunts.hypothesis: An attacker with administrative credentials elevates an auxiliary user account or service principal by granting Global Administrator or other sensitive tenant roles to secure persistent access.
hunts.logic_summary: Monitors Entra ID AuditLogs for successful role assignment operations under RoleManagement where the assigned role is a sensitive tier-0 directory administrative role.
false_positives: Legitimate scheduled role activations through Privileged Identity Management (PIM) by approved administrators
New IT staff onboarding or role re-assignment during business reorganizations
tuning: Whitelist automated PIM activations if pre-approved change ticket metadata is present
Alert on permanent role assignments rather than time-limited eligible activations
triage_steps: Contact the initiating administrator (Actor) to confirm if they authorized the role grant
Check whether the target account had recent anomalous logins or MFA resets
Verify if a corresponding IT change management ticket was logged for the privileged role change
hunts.response: Remove the assigned privileged role immediately via Entra ID, disable the target account, and audit all activities performed by both accounts in the preceding 48 hours.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1098.003 Account Manipulation - Additional Cloud Roles
Microsoft Entra Audit Activity Reference

hunts.query:
// HB-ID-006 | T1098.003 | Highly privileged directory role assigned in Entra ID
// Hypothesis: An attacker assigns Global Administrator or other sensitive directory roles to a rogue account to solidify persistence and tenant-wide control.
let lookback = 7d;
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Category =~ "RoleManagement"
| where OperationName in~ (
    "Add member to role",
    "Add eligible member to role",
    "Add member to role in PIM completed"
)
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend RoleName = tostring(TargetResources[0].modifiedProperties[1].newValue)
| extend TargetUser = tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName)
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| where RoleName has_any (
    "Global Administrator",
    "Privileged Role Administrator",
    "Security Administrator",
    "Exchange Administrator",
    "User Administrator"
)
| project
    TimeGenerated,
    OperationName,
    RoleName,
    TargetUser,
    Actor,
    ResultDescription,
    TargetResources
| order by TimeGenerated desc

hunts.title: RDP lateral movement fan-out to multiple internal endpoints
hunts.hypothesis: An adversary with valid credentials utilizes Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) to rapidly access and compromise multiple endpoints across the corporate network from a single staging system.
hunts.logic_summary: Aggregates successful RemoteInteractive (RDP) logons from DeviceLogonEvents grouped by source IP and account in 2-hour windows, alerting when connections fan out to 4 or more distinct target hostnames.

parameters.name: window
parameters.description: Tumbling time bucket window for grouping RDP sessions

parameters.name: minHosts
parameters.description: Minimum number of unique target endpoints accessed

false_positives: Centralized IT administrative jump boxes / bastion hosts used by authorized helpdesk technicians
Automated enterprise vulnerability management or patch deployment scanners
tuning: Whitelist dedicated corporate Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) and jump hosts by RemoteIP
Raise minHosts threshold if system administrators legitimately connect to multiple servers concurrently
triage_steps: Verify whether the AccountName belongs to an authorized IT systems administrator
Identify the RemoteIP and examine telemetry on the source machine for evidence of prior malware infection
Check what commands were executed on the target endpoints immediately following the RDP sessions
hunts.response: Isolate the source workstation, terminate active RDP sessions across all affected targets, and temporarily disable the compromised user account pending credential rotation.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1021.001 Remote Services - Remote Desktop Protocol
Microsoft Defender Advanced Hunting DeviceLogonEvents

hunts.query:
// HB-LM-001 | T1021.001 | RDP lateral movement fan-out to multiple internal endpoints
// Hypothesis: An attacker uses Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) with administrative credentials from a single compromised internal host to fan out and log into multiple target machines across the network.
let lookback = 3d;
let window = 2h;
let minHosts = 4;
DeviceLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where ActionType =~ "LogonSuccess"
| where LogonType =~ "RemoteInteractive" // Type 10 (Remote Desktop Protocol)
| where isnotempty(RemoteIP)
| summarize
    TargetHostsCount = dcount(DeviceName),
    TargetHosts = make_set(DeviceName, 10),
    FirstLogon = min(Timestamp),
    LastLogon = max(Timestamp),
    AdminSessionCount = countif(IsLocalAdmin == true)
    by RemoteIP, RemoteDeviceName, AccountName, bin(Timestamp, window)
| where TargetHostsCount >= minHosts
| project
    Timestamp,
    RemoteIP,
    RemoteDeviceName,
    AccountName,
    TargetHostsCount,
    AdminSessionCount,
    TargetHosts,
    FirstLogon,
    LastLogon
| order by AdminSessionCount desc, TargetHostsCount desc

hunts.title: Remote service or PsExec-like execution spawned by services.exe
hunts.hypothesis: An adversary moves laterally by using PsExec or remote service creation tools to execute interactive shells or payload binaries on remote systems spawned directly by services.exe.
hunts.logic_summary: Filters DeviceProcessEvents for known remote execution service wrappers (psexesvc, paexec) or instances where the Windows Service Control Manager (services.exe) directly spawns an interactive shell.
false_positives: Legitimate IT remote administration batch scripts utilizing Sysinternals PsExec
Enterprise monitoring or remote management and maintenance (RMM) software agents
tuning: Allow-list approved administrative automation tools executed exclusively by designated domain admin service accounts
Correlate with DeviceNetworkEvents to verify incoming SMB connections on port 445
triage_steps: Inspect ProcessCommandLine to see what commands or secondary scripts were executed
Identify the source machine that initiated the remote service via network and logon telemetry
Check whether the user account executing the command has authorized administrative permissions
hunts.response: Terminate the remote process, disable the compromised administrative account, isolate the target machine, and inspect the originating system for primary infection vectors.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1569.002 System Services - Service Execution
Microsoft Defender Advanced Hunting DeviceProcessEvents

hunts.query:
// HB-LM-002 | T1569.002 | Remote service or PsExec-like execution spawned by services.exe
// Hypothesis: An attacker uses PsExec, PaExec, or remote service installation to spawn command shells on remote endpoints for lateral movement.
let lookback = 7d;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where FileName in~ ("psexesvc.exe", "paexec.exe", "winexesvc.exe", "remotesvc.exe")
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "services.exe" and FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "mshta.exe"))
| project
    Timestamp,
    DeviceName,
    AccountName,
    FileName,
    ProcessCommandLine,
    InitiatingProcessFileName,
    InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
    ProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by Timestamp desc

hunts.title: SMB admin share access fan-out to multiple internal hosts
hunts.hypothesis: An adversary who has compromised internal administrative credentials uses SMB (TCP port 445) to connect to multiple target machines in rapid succession to stage payloads or execute remote tasks.
hunts.logic_summary: Aggregates successful outbound connections on port 445 from DeviceNetworkEvents grouped by source host and initiating process in 1-hour windows, alerting when connections reach 5 or more distinct internal IPs.

parameters.name: minTargets
parameters.description: Minimum number of unique target IPs on port 445

false_positives: Enterprise vulnerability management scanners (Nessus, Qualys) performing authenticated credentialed scans
Centralized domain file servers or automated backup servers communicating with endpoints
tuning: Whitelist verified corporate vulnerability scanner IP addresses using a Sentinel watchlist
Exclude trusted domain controller replication and dedicated enterprise file servers
triage_steps: Identify the InitiatingProcessFileName and CommandLine on the source machine (e.g. net.exe, powershell.exe, impacket)
Inspect target machines for corresponding 4624/4672 logon events or remote service creations
Check whether the user account has legitimate administrative responsibilities over all targeted endpoints
hunts.response: Isolate the source endpoint via Defender for Endpoint API, block outbound SMB lateral movement, and rotate passwords for the affected administrative account.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1021.002 Remote Services - SMB/Windows Admin Shares
Microsoft Defender Advanced Hunting DeviceNetworkEvents

hunts.query:
// HB-LM-003 | T1021.002 | SMB admin share access fan-out to multiple internal hosts
// Hypothesis: An attacker uses SMB (port 445) from an interactive script or utility to connect to admin shares (C$, ADMIN$) across multiple systems for lateral movement or staging.
let lookback = 3d;
let window = 1h;
let minTargets = 5;
let benignSystemProcs = dynamic(["System", "spoolsv.exe", "SearchIndexer.exe", "dfsrs.exe"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where ActionType =~ "ConnectionSuccess"
| where RemotePort == 445
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (benignSystemProcs))
| extend HasAdminSharePattern = iff(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("C$", "ADMIN$", "IPC$", "net use"), true, false)
| summarize
    DistinctTargets = dcount(RemoteIP),
    TargetIPs = make_set(RemoteIP, 10),
    FirstConnection = min(Timestamp),
    LastConnection = max(Timestamp),
    AdminShareHits = countif(HasAdminSharePattern)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, window)
| where DistinctTargets >= minTargets
| project
    Timestamp,
    SourceDevice = DeviceName,
    InitiatingProcessFileName,
    InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
    InitiatingProcessAccountName,
    DistinctTargets,
    TargetIPs,
    AdminShareHits,
    FirstConnection,
    LastConnection
| order by AdminShareHits desc, DistinctTargets desc

hunts.title: Persistence via Windows registry Run or RunOnce keys
hunts.hypothesis: An adversary creates or modifies values under the Run or RunOnce registry keys pointing to a script engine or untrusted directory so that their malware maintains persistence across system reboots or user logons.
hunts.logic_summary: Monitors DeviceRegistryEvents for RegistryValueSet operations targeting CurrentVersion\Run or RunOnce where the stored command value references suspicious scripting interpreters or staging directories.
false_positives: Legitimate enterprise software updates or new software installations adding auto-start launchers
Antivirus or VPN client updater binaries writing to ProgramData
tuning: Allow-list approved vendor executable paths located strictly under C:\Program Files or C:\Program Files (x86)
Filter out trusted administrative install processes such as msiexec.exe when initiating process signer is trusted
triage_steps: Inspect RegistryValueData to see the exact binary or command line scheduled for auto-run
Verify if the file exists on disk and calculate its SHA256 hash using DeviceFileEvents
Determine if the InitiatingProcess was an interactive user shell or an unexpected process
hunts.response: Delete the malicious registry value, remove the referenced executable from disk, and perform a full host scan.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1547.001 Boot or Logon Autostart Execution - Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
Microsoft Defender Advanced Hunting DeviceRegistryEvents

hunts.query:
// HB-PS-001 | T1547.001 | Persistence via Windows registry Run or RunOnce keys
// Hypothesis: An attacker establishes persistence by modifying registry Run/RunOnce keys so their payload executes upon user logon.
let lookback = 7d;
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where ActionType =~ "RegistryValueSet"
| where RegistryKey has_any (
    @"\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run",
    @"\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce"
)
| where RegistryValueData has_any (
    "powershell", "cmd.exe", "wscript", "cscript", "mshta", "rundll32", "regsvr32",
    @"\AppData\Local\Temp", @"\Users\Public\", @"C:\ProgramData\"
)
| project
    Timestamp,
    DeviceName,
    RegistryKey,
    RegistryValueName,
    RegistryValueData,
    PreviousRegistryValueData,
    InitiatingProcessFileName,
    InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
    InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

hunts.title: Scheduled task created by uncommon parent process
hunts.hypothesis: An adversary creates a Windows scheduled task via schtasks.exe spawned from an interactive shell, script interpreter, or Office application to establish persistent execution or schedule lateral movement.
hunts.logic_summary: Detects process creation of schtasks.exe with /create in its arguments where the parent initiating process is a shell, script host, or office document rather than typical system installation binaries.
false_positives: Enterprise deployment scripts or IT automation batch files executing schtasks /create during software rollouts
Developer environment scripts setting up local recurring background jobs
tuning: Whitelist approved administrative IT deployment batch scripts executed from dedicated management shares
Require elevated integrity level or filter by specific task paths (e.g. tasks created under \Microsoft\Windows\)
triage_steps: Analyze ProcessCommandLine to extract the scheduled task name (/tn), binary path (/tr), and frequency (/sc)
Inspect the task action payload to determine if it downloads a remote script or launches a malicious executable
Correlate with InitiatingProcessCommandLine to see how the parent shell received the command
hunts.response: Delete the rogue scheduled task using schtasks /delete /tn <TaskName> /f, remove the associated payload from disk, and isolate the host for forensic imaging.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1053.005 Scheduled Task/Job - Scheduled Task
Microsoft Defender Advanced Hunting DeviceProcessEvents

hunts.query:
// HB-PS-002 | T1053.005 | Scheduled task created by uncommon parent process
// Hypothesis: An attacker uses schtasks.exe to establish persistence or execute delayed tasks, spawned from a command-line script or office document.
let lookback = 7d;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/create", "-create")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (
    "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "cmd.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe",
    "winword.exe", "excel.exe", "mshta.exe", "rundll32.exe"
)
| project
    Timestamp,
    DeviceName,
    AccountName,
    ProcessCommandLine,
    InitiatingProcessFileName,
    InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
    InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
    ProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by Timestamp desc

hunts.title: New Windows service installed pointing to untrusted path
hunts.hypothesis: An adversary creates a new Windows service executing binaries from user-writable directories or invoking script interpreters to gain persistent, elevated execution as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM.
hunts.logic_summary: Searches DeviceEvents for ServiceInstalled events where the installed service binary path resides in staging directories (AppData, Temp, Users\Public, ProgramData) or references script engines.
false_positives: Legitimate enterprise applications installing background helper services in ProgramData (e.g. Chrome / Edge update services)
Developer tooling creating local debugging or microservice instances
tuning: Whitelist digitally signed executables from trusted software vendors
Suppress services created during scheduled software deployment maintenance windows
triage_steps: Inspect the ServiceFileName and ServiceName to determine the purpose and origin of the binary
Check the binary SHA256 hash against threat intelligence databases using DeviceFileEvents
Identify which account and process created the service
hunts.response: Stop and delete the malicious service (sc.exe stop <ServiceName> && sc.exe delete <ServiceName>), remove the binary, and inspect the endpoint for lateral movement activity.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1543.003 Create or Modify System Process - Windows Service
Microsoft Defender Advanced Hunting DeviceEvents

hunts.query:
// HB-PS-003 | T1543.003 | New Windows service installed pointing to untrusted path
// Hypothesis: An attacker installs a rogue Windows service to establish persistence with SYSTEM-level execution privileges.
let lookback = 7d;
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where ActionType =~ "ServiceInstalled"
| extend ServiceName = coalesce(tostring(AdditionalFields.ServiceName), tostring(AdditionalFields.Name))
| extend ServiceBinary = coalesce(
    tostring(AdditionalFields.ServiceFileName),
    tostring(AdditionalFields.ImagePath),
    FileName
)
| where ServiceBinary has_any (
    @"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Users\Public\", @"C:\ProgramData\",
    "powershell", "cmd.exe", "mshta", "rundll32", "certutil"
)
| project
    Timestamp,
    DeviceName,
    AccountName,
    ServiceName,
    ServiceBinary,
    InitiatingProcessFileName,
    InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
    AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc

hunts.title: WMI Event Subscription Persistence
hunts.hypothesis: An adversary creates a permanent Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) event filter and consumer binding to establish stealthy persistence, executing malicious code with SYSTEM privileges whenever target system events fire.
hunts.logic_summary: Inspects DeviceEvents for WMI subscription creation actions (WmiEventFilterCreated, WmiEventConsumerCreated, WmiEventConsumerToFilterCreated), parsing consumer names, trigger queries, and initiating process telemetry.
false_positives: Enterprise endpoint management agents (e.g. SCCM/MECM, Dell Command, HP Support Assistant) registering health filters
Antivirus and EDR software maintaining local system state watchdogs
tuning: Whitelist known IT management consumer names matching verified vendor binaries
Suppress benign OEM hardware telemetry monitors signed by trusted root certificates
triage_steps: Inspect the CommandLine and Query within AdditionalFields to identify the payload or script being executed
Determine whether the Consumer is a CommandLineEventConsumer (runs an EXE/script) or ActiveScriptEventConsumer (executes VBScript/JScript)
Trace the InitiatingProcessCommandLine that installed the subscription (e.g. wmic.exe, powershell.exe, or mofcomp.exe)
Check the device for persistence removal using Get-CimInstance -Namespace root\subscription
hunts.response: Remove the malicious WMI filter, consumer, and binding objects via PowerShell CIM commands, isolate the infected host, and conduct memory and disk forensic analysis.

hunts.title: Volume Shadow Copy deletion and system recovery inhibition
hunts.hypothesis: An active ransomware operator or automated ransomware payload inhibits system recovery by purging Volume Shadow Copies and system backups via vssadmin, wmic, or bcdedit immediately prior to encrypting files.
hunts.logic_summary: Scans DeviceProcessEvents for invocations of native recovery utilities (vssadmin, wmic, wbadmin, bcdedit, PowerShell) with command-line switches specifically targeting shadow copy deletion, catalog removal, or boot recovery disabling.
false_positives: Rare legitimate disk management operations or proprietary enterprise backup agents that clean up temporary snapshots
Operating system re-imaging scripts running in dedicated staging environments
tuning: Allow-list approved enterprise backup agent service binaries (e.g. Veeam, Commvault) if they utilize vssadmin with strict parent process validation
Exclude lab environments dedicated to OS image deployment
triage_steps: Treat as a critical P1 incident: immediately check if multiple endpoints are exhibiting this behavior concurrently
Review DeviceFileEvents for mass file renaming, file drops with unusual extensions (.lockbit, .blackcat), or ransom notes
Inspect InitiatingProcessFileName and CommandLine to find the parent process or malware loader responsible
hunts.response: Immediately isolate the host from the network using Defender for Endpoint API, trigger an automated investigation, and page the incident response on-call team to contain potential lateral ransomware spreading.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1490 Inhibit System Recovery
Microsoft Defender Threat Analytics - Ransomware Defense

hunts.query:
// HB-RW-001 | T1490 | Volume Shadow Copy deletion and system recovery inhibition
// Hypothesis: Ransomware or a destructive attacker deletes Volume Shadow Copies and disables Windows recovery options to prevent file restoration prior to encryption.
let lookback = 3d;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where (FileName =~ "vssadmin.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("delete", "shadows"))
     or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("shadowcopy", "delete"))
     or (FileName =~ "wbadmin.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("delete", "catalog"))
     or (FileName =~ "bcdedit.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("recoveryenabled", "bootstatuspolicy"))
     or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Delete-WmiObject", "Win32_ShadowCopy"))
| project
    Timestamp,
    DeviceName,
    AccountName,
    FileName,
    ProcessCommandLine,
    InitiatingProcessFileName,
    InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
    InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
    ProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by Timestamp desc

hunts.title: Ransomware Mass File Rename with Encrypted Extension
hunts.hypothesis: A ransomware binary is actively encrypting files across user documents and network shares, renaming files in rapid succession and appending known encryption extensions or converting user documents (.docx, .pdf, .xlsx) to arbitrary extensions, serving as a critical behavioral indicator of encryption.
hunts.logic_summary: Monitors DeviceFileEvents for FileRenamed operations, detecting rapid bursts exceeding 20 file renames within 10 minutes by untrusted processes where target document extensions transition into known ransomware extensions or non-document formats.

parameters.name: renameThreshold
parameters.description: Minimum number of renamed files within the window

false_positives: Software installation or patch update routines creating temporary backup files
Developer batch build scripts or archive compression utilities renaming build artifacts
tuning: Exclude verified enterprise backup utilities, source code compilers (e.g. msbuild.exe, devenv.exe), and sync agents
Note that mass file renaming is a behavioral indicator, not absolute proof of encryption; correlate with shadow copy deletion and ransom note file creations
triage_steps: Inspect InitiatingProcessFileName and InitiatingProcessCommandLine to identify the encrypting binary or script
Examine SampleNewFiles to determine whether a ransom note (e.g. README.txt, HOW_TO_DECRYPT.txt) was dropped nearby
Immediately check if other hosts on the same network subnet are reporting similar mass rename bursts
Review DeviceNetworkEvents from the source process for outbound command-and-control communication
hunts.response: Immediately isolate the host from the network via Defender for Endpoint portal, kill the initiating process tree, preserve volatile RAM and disk forensic artifacts, and begin recovery from off-site immutable backups.

hunts.title: Safe-Mode or Boot Recovery Disabled via Bcdedit
hunts.hypothesis: An adversary executes bcdedit.exe commands to disable Windows Startup Repair and boot error handling immediately prior to executing ransomware encryption, preventing victim machines from recovering automatically.
hunts.logic_summary: Filters DeviceProcessEvents for invocations of bcdedit.exe where command-line switches include 'recoveryenabled', 'bootstatuspolicy', or 'ignoreallfailures', classifying the tampered boot configuration.
false_positives: Enterprise OS imaging, system deployment scripts, or hypervisor template provisioning workflows
Authorized system administrators testing diagnostic boot environments
tuning: Whitelist dedicated corporate deployment scripts executing from approved imaging servers
Suppress alerts during pre-scheduled bare-metal workstation rollout windows
triage_steps: Review the full ProcessCommandLine to observe the exact configuration parameters modified
Inspect InitiatingProcessFileName and InitiatingProcessCommandLine (e.g. cmd.exe launched from a batch script or malicious document)
Search DeviceProcessEvents on the same host within +/- 30 minutes for shadow copy deletion (vssadmin, wmic shadowcopy)
Check for suspicious child processes or unauthorized persistence mechanisms installed concurrently
hunts.response: Immediately isolate the host from the corporate network, re-enable startup repair using 'bcdedit /set {default} recoveryenabled Yes', and trigger a full Defender antivirus and EDR remediation scan.
